title: Azure RBAC: built-in roles, scopes and interpreting access
learningObjective: Pick the smallest built-in role that does the job, give it at the right level, and explain why someone can or can't do something.

prerequisites.text: Hierarchy of management groups, subscriptions and resource groups (AZ-900)

foundation: Azure role-based access control (RBAC) answers one question: who can do what, where.

Who is a security principal: a user, a group, a service principal or a managed identity. What is a role definition: a list of allowed operations such as 'restart a virtual machine'. Where is a scope: a management group, a subscription, a resource group or a single resource.
A role assignment ties those three together. Assign a role at a resource group and it applies to every resource inside it. Scopes inherit downward, never upward.

Four built-in roles show up everywhere: Owner (everything, including granting access), Contributor (everything except granting access), Reader (look but do not touch) and User Access Administrator (manage who has access).
engineer: Inside a role: Actions, the things it allows; NotActions, things taken away from Actions; DataActions and NotDataActions, the same for data such as blobs; AssignableScopes, where the role can be used. What one role allows = Actions minus NotActions.
NotActions don't block anything: they only remove actions from that one role. If another role gives the action, the user can do it.
Roles add up: a user's access is everything from all their roles, including roles given to their groups, at this level and every level above it.

Why Contributor can't give access: Contributor allows everything ('*') except Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write, Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete and Microsoft.Authorization/elevateAccess/Action. So it can't create role assignments or policy assignments.
Deny assignments: the only thing that beats a role. You can't create them yourself. Azure features such as Managed Applications and deployment stacks create them.

Two kinds of roles: Azure roles control Azure resources (VMs, storage, networks); Entra roles control the directory (users, groups, licences). A Global Administrator can't see Azure resources by default. They can 'elevate', which gives them User Access Administrator at the very top (/).

Data access is separate: Owner of a storage account can't read blobs with Entra sign-in. You need a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader (it uses DataActions). The portal may still show data, because it can fall back to the account keys.
Changes take a few minutes: new role assignments need fresh sign-in tokens. Signing out and in again gets a new token.

Who can give roles: anyone with Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, which means Owner, User Access Administrator, or Role Based Access Control Administrator (this one can be limited with conditions).

example.title: Just enough access for an operations team
body: The operations team must restart and resize VMs in the Prod subscription. They must not change networking or give access to others.
Give Virtual Machine Contributor to the Ops team group, on the subscription. Every VM in every resource group gets it, including VMs created later.
A contractor only needs to look at resources in rg-web. Give Reader to the contractor's guest account on rg-web, not on the subscription.
Give roles to groups, not to people. Then access stays right when staff change, and you stay under the limit on role assignments per subscription.

prerequisites: The user, group or identity exists in the Entra tenant the subscription trusts
permissions: Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write at that level: Owner, User Access Administrator, or Role Based Access Control Administrator
limits: Up to 4,000 role assignments per subscription
Up to 500 role assignments per management group
Management groups go up to six levels below the root (not counting the root or subscriptions)
Role changes can take a few minutes to work
portal: Open the scope (management group, subscription, resource group or resource) > Access control (IAM).
Roles tab: inspect a built-in role's permissions (View > Permissions/JSON).
Add > Add role assignment: choose the role, then Members (user, group, service principal or managed identity), then Review + assign.
Check access tab: select a user to list their effective assignments at this scope, including inherited ones and those received via groups.
Role assignments tab: filter by scope to see 'This resource' vs 'Inherited'.
configuration.cli:
az role definition list --name "Virtual Machine Contributor" --query "[0].permissions"
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id <ops-group-object-id> --assignee-principal-type Group \
  --role "Virtual Machine Contributor" --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id>
az role assignment create --assignee contractor@fabrikam.com --role Reader \
  --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-web
az role assignment list --assignee ana@contoso.com --all --include-inherited --include-groups -o table
configuration.powershell:
Get-AzRoleDefinition -Name "Virtual Machine Contributor" | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Actions
$ops = Get-AzADGroup -DisplayName "Ops team"
New-AzRoleAssignment -ObjectId $ops.Id -RoleDefinitionName "Virtual Machine Contributor" -Scope "/subscriptions/<sub-id>"
New-AzRoleAssignment -SignInName contractor@fabrikam.com -RoleDefinitionName Reader -ResourceGroupName rg-web
Get-AzRoleAssignment -SignInName ana@contoso.com -ExpandPrincipalGroups

lab.objective: Grant Ana exactly the access she needs, and explain every allowed or denied request.
steps: Check whether Ana can restart vm-web-01 with no assignments. Read the reason.
Assign Virtual Machine Contributor to the Ops team group at the subscription. Re-check: the grant is inherited and arrives via the group.
Have Ana try to create a role assignment on rg-web. It fails: VM Contributor does not include Microsoft.Authorization actions.
Assign Contributor to Ana at rg-web and try again. It still fails: Contributor's NotActions exclude role assignment writes.
Remove the over-broad Contributor assignment to restore least privilege.
expected: Inherited allow via group for restart.
Contributor blocked by NotActions for roleAssignments/write.
Final state: only the group VM Contributor assignment remains.

validation.text: Produced an allow that was inherited from a parent scope
Ended with no Owner or Contributor assignments for Ana

failureScenarios: Assigning at a child scope and expecting access at the parent.
Assigning an Entra role (e.g. User Administrator) and expecting Azure resource access.
cleanup: Simulation only: use Restart to clear assignments.
lab.cost: None. Runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: A user was just given a role but still gets AuthorizationFailed.
troubleshooting.cause: Their sign-in token is old and doesn't include the new role yet.
troubleshooting.fix: Wait a few minutes, or sign out and in. In the CLI, run az account clear and then az login.

troubleshooting.symptom: A Contributor can't give a role to a managed identity during a deployment.
troubleshooting.cause: Contributor isn't allowed to create role assignments.
troubleshooting.fix: Give the deploying identity Role Based Access Control Administrator (with conditions if you like) or User Access Administrator at that level.

troubleshooting.symptom: A Global Administrator can't see any subscriptions.
troubleshooting.cause: Entra roles don't give access to Azure resources.
troubleshooting.fix: Elevate access for a short time (Entra ID > Properties > Access management for Azure resources), give the right Azure role, then turn the elevation off.

troubleshooting.symptom: An Owner gets 403 reading blobs with --auth-mode login.
troubleshooting.cause: Owner covers managing the account, not reading the data.
troubleshooting.fix: Give Storage Blob Data Reader or Contributor on the account or container.

troubleshooting.symptom: Even an Owner can't delete something.
troubleshooting.cause: A delete lock (CanNotDelete) or a deny assignment is in place.
troubleshooting.fix: Check Locks, and the Deny assignments tab in Access control (IAM).

comparisons.difference: They control the directory (users, groups, apps), for the whole tenant or an administrative unit. They don't control Azure resources.
Policy checks what a resource looks like. RBAC checks who can do something. A request can pass RBAC and still be blocked by Policy.
AWS has Deny statements that always win. Azure roles have no Deny: NotActions only take actions away, and only Azure itself creates deny assignments.

misconceptions.reality: No. They only take it out of that one role. Another role can still allow it.

misconceptions.myth: Owner on a VM gives access to its resource group.
misconceptions.reality: No. Access flows down to child resources, never up.

misconceptions.myth: A Global Administrator is automatically Owner of every subscription.
misconceptions.reality: No. Only after they elevate their access, and that gives User Access Administrator at the top level.

misconceptions.myth: Contributor can give access to others.
misconceptions.reality: No. That needs Owner, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator.

architectureDecisions: Assign at the highest level that is still right: many small assignments on single resources are hard to check.
Give roles to groups, not people: add or remove a person from the group instead of changing roles.
Pick a job role, not Contributor: use roles such as Virtual Machine Contributor or Network Contributor. Make a custom role only when no built-in role fits.
Make powerful roles temporary: with Privileged Identity Management (PIM), people turn on Owner or User Access Administrator only when they need it.

walkthrough.subtitle: Answer three questions for every permission: who, what, and where.

steps.label: Too much access
steps.title: Everyone is Owner
body: In a small team, it is tempting to make everyone Owner of the subscription. Then an intern deletes the production database.
You need to give each person only what they need, only where they need it.

steps.label: Who + what
steps.title: Who and what
body: Who is a security principal: a user, a group, a service principal (an app) or a managed identity.
What is a role definition: a list of allowed actions, such as read anything, or restart VMs.

steps.label: Where
steps.title: Where: the scope
body: A scope is a management group, a subscription, a resource group or one resource. Access given at a scope flows down to everything below it, never up.

callout.text: Assign at the smallest scope that does the job, usually a resource group.

steps.label: Key roles
steps.title: Four roles you must know
body: Owner: full access, including giving access to others. Contributor: create and manage everything, but cannot give access. Reader: view only. User Access Administrator: manage access only.
Many specific roles exist too, such as Virtual Machine Contributor.

callout.text: Contributor cannot assign roles. That needs Owner, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator.

steps.label: Assignment
steps.title: A role assignment ties it together
body: A role assignment = principal + role + scope. Access adds up: Ana's effective access is all her assignments plus those of every group she is in, at this scope and above.
Use Access control (IAM) > Check access to see exactly what someone has, and why.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: RBAC in one minute
body: Who + what + where, with the smallest scope.
recap: Principal: user, group, service principal, managed identity
Role definition: list of allowed actions
Scope inherits downward: MG > subscription > RG > resource
Owner / Contributor / Reader / User Access Administrator
Access is additive; use Check access

handsOn.title: Give Ana Reader on one resource group and prove it
handsOn.cost: Free. Role assignments and empty resource groups cost nothing.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.
Ana Lab from the users lab, and her password.

steps.do: Open Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Access control (IAM) > + Add > Add role assignment.
steps.see: A list of roles with a search box.

steps.do: Search for Reader, select it, then Next. Select + Select members, choose Ana Lab, then Review + assign twice.

steps.see: Ana Lab listed with role Reader and scope 'This resource'.

steps.do: Select Check access, search for Ana Lab and open her.
steps.see: Her Reader assignment on this resource group, and any inherited from above (none yet).

steps.do: In a private browser window sign in to portal.azure.com as Ana. Open Resource groups.
steps.tip: Azure requires multifactor authentication for portal sign-in, so the first time Ana is asked to set up the Microsoft Authenticator app (or another method). New role assignments can take a few minutes; if nothing shows, sign out and in again.

steps.do: As Ana, open rg-az104-lab and try + Create > Storage account, and try to create it.
steps.see: The deployment fails with an authorization error: Reader cannot create resources.

steps.do: As yourself, change Ana's role to Contributor (remove Reader, add Contributor) and repeat step 6 with a storage account name, then cancel before creating.
steps.see: Ana can now reach the Review page. Contributor can create, Reader cannot.

check: Check access shows Ana's role on rg-az104-lab.
You saw a Reader blocked from creating a resource.
cleanup: Remove Ana's role assignment: rg-az104-lab > Access control (IAM) > Role assignments > select > Delete.
